newsitem.title: UK: Stroke of fate saved Uday Hussein - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Stroke of fate saved Uday Hussein - newspaper.

text.p: The eldest son of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein only survived last year's assassination attempt because of a last minute stroke of luck, the Independent newspaper reported on Tuesday.

Assassination squad leader Ismail Othman said in an interview that Uday Hussein escaped death by swapping places with the front passenger in his car moments before gunmen opened fire, aiming for the driver.
Hussein escaped with serious injuries in the attack in Baghdad's wealthy district of al-Mansour in December 1996.
Othman said his group al-Nadhad ('The Awakening') plotted the ambush after deciding that kidnapping Hussein was too dangerous.

"We decided to kill Uday two years ago," said Othman, who lives in hiding in Europe. "We thought the regime had four pillars: Saddam, Uday...his younger brother Qusai, and their cousin Ali Hassan al-Majid. Of these, Uday was the easiest to get to."

When they discovered Hussein would be going to a party in Mansur, the group picked a crossroads he would have to pass through, in one of three identical white Mercedes he used to confuse potential attackers.

As the convoy drew near, one of the four gunmen hurled a grenade at it. He then raced towards the first car, firing a Kalashnikov assault rifle at the driver, expecting Hussein to be in the driver's seat.
Only when a second gunman drew nearer did the four realise they had missed their target, and they quickly opened fire on the other three cars.
Eight bullets tore into Hussein, injuring both legs. One bullet is still lodged in his spine.
Othman said the gunmen escaped by car into Iraq's western desert.

Hussein has undergone several operations since the attack. Although he recently left hospital saying he was recovering, many Iraqis believe he is too crippled to succeed his 60-year-old father, Iraq's iron dictator for more than a quarter of a century.
Al-Nahdah was formed in 1991 in the wake of the Gulf War which left Iraq with a shattered infrastructure and estranged by the United Nations' sanctions.

Othman said the group, largely made up of Baghdad students, believed it was not feasible to try and kill Saddam Hussein, who is well protected and whose whereabouts are a fiercely guarded secret at all times.
